si_4_title: Toward Understanding Autism Heterogeneity: Identifying Clinical Subgroups and Neuroanatomical Deviations
sc_1_study_objective: To parse clinical and neuroanatomical heterogeneity in autism by combining clustering of clinical features with normative modeling based on neuroanatomical measures (cortical thickness [CT] and subcortical volume) within the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange data sets.

caa_7_association_analysis: Group comparisons of deviation overlap maps using permutation tests with FDR correction. SVM classification to test biological separability.
caa_8_key_findings_brief: Two clinical subgroups were identified in autistic individuals, primarily differing in restrictive and repetitive behaviors (RRBs), and these subgroups showed more homogeneous neuroanatomical deviation profiles compared to the entire autism group.
caa_9_key_findings_detailed: Model-based clustering of ADOS-G scores identified two stable subgroups: a high-RRB subgroup and a low-RRB subgroup. Normative modeling of cortical thickness and subcortical volume revealed significant heterogeneity across all autistic individuals. However, the clinical subgroups showed increased homogeneity (spatial overlap of extreme deviations). The high-RRB subgroup had greater overlap of positive deviations in the cerebellum, while the low-RRB subgroup had greater overlap of negative deviations in regions like the postcentral gyrus and fusiform cortex. Despite increased homogeneity, SVM classification accuracy did not improve for the subgroups compared to the whole autism group, suggesting substantial remaining heterogeneity.

caa_10_key_limitations.answer: 1. Primary analysis was limited to males due to small female sample size. 2. Clinical subgrouping was based on broad ADOS subscores, not item-level data, which may obscure finer-grained clinical differences. 3. The study did not account for co-occurring conditions. 4. Substantial within-subgroup heterogeneity remained (equifinality).
caa_10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Further limitations have to be taken into account. Due to limited power, we focused in primary analyses on males only...Both social communication dif /uniFB01 culties and RRBs are broad, multifaceted categories comprising different lower- and higher-order subcomponents that we were not able to differentiate between given the limitations of the ABIDE dataset...Finally, it has to be pointed out that heterogeneity in clinical pro /uniFB01 les extends to level of cognitive functioning, language abilities and co-occurring conditions that are common in autism...While our results con /uniFB01 rm that subgrouping increases homogeneity, we acknowledge that there remains substantial between subject heterogeneity within the clinical subgroups.

caa_11_application_notes: The study combined data-driven clinical clustering with normative modeling to investigate if reducing clinical heterogeneity leads to more homogeneous neurobiological profiles, providing a framework for parsing heterogeneity in ASD.
gn_1_general_note: The study provides a good example of using normative modeling to move beyond case-control comparisons and investigate individual-level deviations. The code for all analyses is publicly available on GitHub.
